walkthroughs.body_html:
Acid-Base Equilibria — a core area of A-Level Chemistry.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Acid-Base Equilibria brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Acid-Base Equilibria.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: For the Haber process N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃ (exothermic), increasing temperature:
options: Increases yield of NH₃
Decreases yield of NH₃
Does not change yield
Doubles yield

mcqs.q: Adding a catalyst to an equilibrium system:
options: Increases yield
Decreases yield
Shifts position to products
Reaches equilibrium faster, same position

mcqs.q: How does a buffer maintain its pH when small amounts of acid are added?
options: A primary alcohol is oxidised to an alkene by losing water.
A buffer prevents any H+ ions from being added to the solution at all.
The conjugate base in the buffer reacts with added H+ to remove it, keeping pH nearly constant.
A buffer destroys added acid by changing it into water vapour.

mcqs.q: What is the product of mild oxidation of a primary alcohol?
options: A primary alcohol is oxidised to an alkene by losing water.
A primary alcohol is oxidised directly to a ketone.
A strong acid is one that has been heated to higher temperature.
An aldehyde (which can be further oxidised to a carboxylic acid).

mcqs.q: What is the difference between a strong acid and a concentrated acid?
options: Strong and concentrated mean the same thing for acids.
A strong acid is one that has been heated to higher temperature.
A strong acid fully dissociates in water; a concentrated acid has a high amount of acid per volume — these are independent properties.
A buffer destroys added acid by changing it into water vapour.
